Vegetation
Native vegetation used primarily for grazing occupies about 22,725 acres of the 25,000 acres expected to be mined. About 8,630 acres support ponderosa pine stands of limited value for timber production. The remaining 2,275 acres are currently used for cropland.
All vegetative cover, including forest, in the mine area and support facilities areas will be removed during the mining operation. The degree of unavoidable adverse impacts will depend upon the rapidity of revegetation, including restoration of forest cover on the area. Reforestation of the area will probably take several decades.
Species composition of plant communities will be altered by mining.

Reestablishment of climax type vegetation, if it can be achieved, will take a considerable period of time, as certain plant species present in the native climax communities are extremely slow to re-enter a disturbed site. Some may never be reestablished due to changes in environmental conditions. As discussed previously, each plant species requires particular environmental conditions, and if these are not present, that plant species will not become established.
The mining project may accelerate timber harvest in the project area. This need not be an adverse effect if proper silvicultural methods are utilized.
